forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 1. For which real numbers $x$ is \\[\\lfloor nx \\rfloor - \\sum_{k=1}^{n} \\frac{\\lfloor kx \\rfloor}{k}\\] maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?

payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The proof correctly uses the defining property of the floor function to obtain m = floor(x) with m <= x < m+1, deduces 0 <= x-m < 1, identifies x-m as frac(x), and concludes x = floor(x) + frac(x) with 0 <= frac(x) < 1. This exactly matches the lemma statement and the assembly role.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer such that m <= x < m + 1. Subtracting m from all parts gives 0 <= x - m < 1. By the definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m. Therefore 0 <= frac(x) < 1, and also x = floor(x) + frac(x). Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.

result_payload.addressed_previous_feedback: Previous vetter feedback confirmed the floor/fractional-part argument was correct; this revision keeps that same proof and states the definition-based steps explicitly.
result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer satisfying m <= x < m + 1. Subtracting m throughout gives 0 <= x - m < 1. By the definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m. Hence 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Also, rearranging the identity frac(x) = x - floor(x) yields x = floor(x) + frac(x). Since x was arbitrary, this holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: Apply the defining inequality for floor(x), identify x-floor(x) with frac(x), and rearrange.
